reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / KDIGO
clinicalPearls: Fanconi syndrome is a generalised defect of proximal tubular reabsorption, so multiple solutes normally reclaimed there are lost into the urine at once
The hallmark laboratory picture combines glycosuria with normal blood glucose, phosphaturia with hypophosphataemia, aminoaciduria, uricosuria, and a proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosis
Phosphate and vitamin D handling are disturbed, producing metabolic bone disease that presents as rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults
In children the commonest cause is inherited cystinosis, whereas in adults acquired causes such as drugs, heavy metals, and monoclonal light chains predominate
Bicarbonate wasting causes a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis, and potassium wasting frequently leads to hypokalaemia
Recognising the full constellation is important because finding one abnormality (e.g. isolated glycosuria) should prompt a search for the others
Treatment is directed at the underlying cause where possible, together with replacement of the wasted solutes: alkali, phosphate, potassium, and active vitamin D as needed
reference.pathophysiology: Fanconi syndrome results from global dysfunction of the proximal convoluted tubule, the segment responsible for reabsorbing the bulk of filtered glucose, amino acids, phosphate, uric acid, bicarbonate, and low-molecular-weight proteins. When proximal transport fails, all of these are wasted in the urine, giving the characteristic combination of glycosuria with euglycaemia, generalised aminoaciduria, hypophosphataemia, hypouricaemia, proximal renal tubular acidosis from bicarbonate loss, and tubular proteinuria. Impaired proximal conversion of vitamin D and phosphate depletion drive the bone disease. Underlying mechanisms include inherited defects of tubular transporters or metabolism (such as cystinosis or Wilson disease), toxic injury from drugs and heavy metals, and deposition of filtered monoclonal light chains, all of which impair the energy-dependent transport machinery of the proximal tubule.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated proximal renal tubular acidosis without full Fanconi features
Diabetes mellitus with glycosuria from hyperglycaemia
Multiple myeloma or other plasma cell dyscrasia
Heavy metal or drug-induced tubular toxicity
additionalInvestigations: Paired urine and blood glucose to demonstrate glycosuria despite normal glycaemia
Serum and urine phosphate, potassium, bicarbonate, and uric acid to document tubular wasting
Urine amino acid screen and low-molecular-weight (tubular) protein measurement
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with free light chains to exclude a plasma cell disorder in adults
Assessment for underlying causes such as cystinosis, Wilson disease, or nephrotoxic drug exposure
Bone imaging or biochemistry when rickets or osteomalacia is suspected
redFlags: Severe hypophosphataemia causing muscle weakness or respiratory compromise
Progressive metabolic bone disease with fractures or deformity
Evidence of an underlying plasma cell dyscrasia in an adult
Declining glomerular filtration suggesting progression of the causative disease
reference.prognosis: Outlook depends on the cause: reversible drug- or toxin-induced Fanconi syndrome may resolve when the offending agent is removed, while inherited forms such as cystinosis and light-chain-related disease can progress to chronic kidney failure. Early replacement therapy prevents or lessens the associated bone disease and growth impairment.
pitfalls: Dismissing glycosuria as diabetes without checking blood glucose or looking for other tubular losses
Missing an underlying paraproteinaemia in an adult presenting with proximal tubular dysfunction
Undertreating the bone disease by giving phosphate without adequate active vitamin D
Failing to review the medication list for a reversible tubulotoxic drug
management: Identify and treat the underlying cause by withdrawing the offending nephrotoxic drug or heavy metal, giving cysteamine for cystinosis, copper chelation or zinc for Wilson disease, or treating an underlying plasma cell disorder
Replace urinary phosphate losses with oral phosphate supplements to treat the metabolic bone disease
Correct the proximal renal tubular acidosis with alkali therapy such as bicarbonate or citrate, often in substantial replacement quantities
Replace potassium and other wasted electrolytes and ensure adequate hydration
Treat rickets or osteomalacia with active vitamin D metabolites alongside phosphate replacement
Monitor renal function, electrolytes and bone health to detect progression to chronic kidney disease
Refer to nephrology and, according to aetiology, to haematology or metabolic specialists
